# A worked record-linkage pipeline {#sec-workflow}

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source("_setup.R")
source("_people.R")
```

This chapter links two files of people end to end: a service **enrolment**
extract and a **claims** extract from a different system, holding many of
the same people. Nothing is pre-cleaned. Every step is one of the
functions in this package, and because the data carry a hidden
`person_id`, every claim made along the way is measured rather than
asserted.

The shape of the problem is always the same:

| Step | Question | Section |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | What is actually in these columns? | @sec-wf-profile |
| 2 | Do the two files agree on types and spelling? | @sec-wf-standardise |
| 3 | Which records are even worth comparing? | @sec-wf-block |
| 4 | How alike is each candidate pair, field by field? | @sec-wf-score |
| 5 | Which pairs do we accept, and which go to a human? | @sec-wf-decide |
| 6 | What is one person's identifier across both files? | @sec-wf-entities |
| 7 | How well did it work, and what did it cost? | @sec-wf-evaluate |

## The two files

```{r}
#| label: data
files  <- people_files(n_enrol = 50000, overlap = 0.6)
enrol  <- files$enrol
claims <- files$claims
c(enrol = nrow(enrol), claims = nrow(claims))
```

The enrolment file is the tidy one: name in three fields, date of birth as
a `Date`, sex as a one-letter code, address in parts, postcode as
zero-padded text.

```{r}
#| label: show-enrol
enrol[1:4, c("enrol_id", "given_name", "middle_name", "surname", "dob", "sex")]
enrol[1:4, c("unit", "number", "street", "street_type", "suburb", "postcode")]
```

The claims file is what a linkage project is usually handed:

```{r}
#| label: show-claims
claims[1:6, ]
```

One name field holding `"SURNAME, Title Given Middle"` in title case, with
doubled and trailing spaces. The date of birth as `"DD/MM/YYYY"` text. Sex
spelled out, sometimes `"Unknown"`, sometimes blank. The address as one
free-text line with a unit prefix and an abbreviated street type. And a
*numeric* postcode, so every Northern Territory postcode has lost its
leading zero.

## Step 1: profile before you match {#sec-wf-profile}

The fastest way to be wrong about a column is to assume you know its
shape. `string_shape()` collapses each value to a character-class pattern,
so the distinct *formats* in a column are a `table()` away:

```{r}
#| label: profile
head(sort(table(string_shape(claims$date_of_birth)), decreasing = TRUE), 3)
head(sort(table(string_shape(claims$patient_name)), decreasing = TRUE), 5)
```

Every date of birth is `99/99/9999`, so one fixed format will parse the
column. The name column has many shapes, which is the signal that it needs
parsing rather than comparing as it stands.

Two more questions worth asking of every incoming column --- how much is
missing, and how much is a placeholder:

```{r}
#| label: profile-quality
c(gender_blank   = mean(!nzchar(claims$gender)),
  gender_unknown = mean(claims$gender == "Unknown"),
  name_untrimmed = mean(claims$patient_name != trimws(claims$patient_name)),
  dob_jan_1      = mean(fgrepl("^01/01/", claims$date_of_birth)),
  postcode_short = mean(fnchar(as.character(claims$postcode)) < 4))
```

About `r "one date of birth in forty-five"` is 1 January --- far more than
the 1-in-365 a real population gives. That is the placeholder a clerk
types when the date is unknown, and a blocking pass on the exact date
would build one huge useless block out of it. @sec-wf-block caps it, and
a real project would set those dates to `NA` instead.

## Step 2: standardise, field by field {#sec-wf-standardise}

The goal is one data frame per file with the same column names, the same
types and the same spelling conventions. Every line below is vectorised
over the whole column.

### The name field

`fupper()` and `fsquish()` first, so nothing downstream has to think about
case or whitespace again; then `fsplit_field()` on the comma; then
`freplace_tokens()` to drop the titles. `freplace_tokens()` matches whole
tokens from a dictionary in one pass, so `"DR"` goes and `"DRUMMOND"`
stays --- which a `gsub("DR", "", ...)` would not manage.

```{r}
#| label: parse-name
titles <- c("MR", "MRS", "MS", "MISS", "DR", "PROF", "REV", "SIR")

name  <- fsquish(fupper(claims$patient_name))
surn  <- ftrimws(fsplit_field(name, ",", 1))
rest  <- fsquish(freplace_tokens(ftrimws(fsplit_field(name, ",", 2)),
                                 titles, rep("", length(titles))))
given  <- fsplit_field(rest, " ", 1)
middle <- fsplit_field(rest, " ", 2)

data.frame(claims$patient_name, surn, given, middle)[1:6, ]
```

Apostrophes and hyphens are the other recurring name problem: the same
person is `O'BRIEN` in one file and `OBRIEN` in the other, `SMITH-JONES`
here and `SMITH JONES` there. Rather than choose, keep the name as given
and compare on a form that ignores the difference. Three functions do
different parts of that job:

```{r}
#| label: name-variants
variants <- c("O'BRIEN", "OBRIEN", "O BRIEN", "o'brien", "D'ARCY", "DARCY",
              "MULLER", "MÜLLER", "SMITH-JONES", "SMITH JONES")
data.frame(variants,
           ascii_fold  = ascii_fold(variants),
           fingerprint = fingerprint(variants),
           letters     = fgsub("[^A-Z]", "", fupper(variants)))
```

`ascii_fold()` is the one that matters for `MÜLLER`: it folds accented
Latin letters to ASCII, so a file that lost its accents still matches one
that kept them. `fingerprint()` (OpenRefine's clustering key) lower-cases,
folds, strips punctuation and **sorts the words**, which is what makes
`SMITH-JONES` and `SMITH JONES` meet --- but note that it keeps `O BRIEN`
apart from `OBRIEN`, because there the space creates a second word rather
than joining two. Stripping to letters alone collapses all four of the
`O'BRIEN` spellings, at the cost of also collapsing names that differ only
in their spacing. A blocking key wants the aggressive form; a *score*
wants the gentle one, which is why `jaro_winkler_tokens()` exists ---
it folds punctuation and spacing inside the comparison, so the raw names
can be compared as they were recorded:

```{r}
#| label: token-compare
jaro_winkler_tokens(c("O'BRIEN", "SMITH-JONES", "O'BRIEN"),
                    c("O BRIEN", "SMITH JONES", "OBRIEN"))
jaro_winkler(c("O'BRIEN", "SMITH-JONES", "O'BRIEN"),
             c("O BRIEN", "SMITH JONES", "OBRIEN"))
```

### The date of birth

`fas.Date()` parses one fixed layout with no locale, no `strptime()` and no
format guessing, and validates the calendar, so an impossible date becomes
`NA` instead of silently rolling over:

```{r}
#| label: parse-dob
dob <- fas.Date(claims$date_of_birth, format = "dmy")
c(parsed = sum(!is.na(dob)), failed = sum(is.na(dob)))

# Strictness is the point: base R's as.Date() guesses, fas.Date() refuses.
fas.Date(c("29/02/2024", "29/02/2023", "31/04/2024", "1/3/2024", NA),
         format = "dmy")
```

2024 is a leap year and 2023 is not; 31 April does not exist; and
`"1/3/2024"` is not `"DD/MM/YYYY"` --- a fixed-width format means
fixed-width. Any of those being `NA` is a finding about the data, which is
what you want at this stage, rather than a wrong date to discover later.

`date_parts()` splits a `Date` into year, month and day columns in one
pass, which is how the cheap partial blocking keys get built:

```{r}
#| label: date-parts
parts <- date_parts(dob)
head(parts, 3)
head(format_date(dob, "y-m"), 3)      # "YYYY-MM", a coarser key
```

### Sex, gender and the vocabulary problem

The two files use different vocabularies for the same field. Map both onto
one, and keep "not recorded" distinct from "disagrees" --- treating an
unknown as a disagreement throws away true matches:

```{r}
#| label: parse-sex
sex_code <- function(x) {
    x <- fupper(ftrimws(as.character(x)))
    out <- rep("U", length(x))
    out[x %in% c("M", "MALE", "1")]   <- "M"
    out[x %in% c("F", "FEMALE", "2")] <- "F"
    out
}
table(raw = claims$gender, coded = sex_code(claims$gender))
```

The comparison that goes with it returns agreement, disagreement, or
neither:

```{r}
#| label: sex-compare
sex_agree <- function(a, b) ifelse(a == "U" | b == "U", 0.5,
                                   as.numeric(a == b))
sex_agree(c("M", "M", "F", "U"), c("M", "F", "F", "F"))
```

### The address

An address line is a street number, a street name, a street type and a
locality, run together with the type abbreviated. Pull the unit off the
front with `fgsub()`, split on the comma, and expand the abbreviations with
a whole-token dictionary --- the same `freplace_tokens()` trick as the
titles, and the reason `"ST KILDA"` does not become `"STREET KILDA"`:

```{r}
#| label: parse-address
street_abbrev <- c("ST", "RD", "AVE", "CT", "PL", "TCE", "PDE", "CRES",
                   "DR", "LN", "HWY", "BLVD")
street_full   <- c("STREET", "ROAD", "AVENUE", "COURT", "PLACE", "TERRACE",
                   "PARADE", "CRESCENT", "DRIVE", "LANE", "HIGHWAY",
                   "BOULEVARD")

raw_addr <- fupper(claims$address_line)
unit     <- fextract("[0-9]+", fextract("^U[0-9]+/", raw_addr))
body     <- fgsub("^U[0-9]+/", "", raw_addr)
street   <- fsquish(freplace_tokens(ftrimws(fsplit_field(body, ",", 1)),
                                    street_abbrev, street_full))
locality <- ftrimws(fgsub(" VIC$", "", fsplit_field(body, ",", 2)))

# Rows with a unit number, so the prefix is visible.
head(data.frame(claims$address_line, unit, street, locality)[!is.na(unit), ], 5)
```

`fextract()` returns the first match of a pattern per element, so the unit
number comes out without a `regmatches()`/`regexpr()` pair. Note that
`"ST KILDA"` survived the dictionary while `"Flinders Cres"` became
`"FLINDERS CRESCENT"`.

### The postcode

A numeric postcode has lost its leading zeros. Pad it back, and validate
rather than assume:

```{r}
#| label: parse-postcode
postcode <- fpad(as.character(claims$postcode), 4, pad = "0")
table(width = fnchar(postcode))
head(sort(table(string_shape(postcode)), decreasing = TRUE), 2)
```

### The standardised files

```{r}
#| label: standardised
claims_std <- data.frame(
    claim_id       = claims$claim_id,
    given_name     = given,
    middle_name    = middle,
    surname        = surn,
    surname_key    = fingerprint(surn),
    dob            = dob,
    sex            = sex_code(claims$gender),
    unit           = unit,
    street_address = street,
    suburb         = locality,
    postcode       = postcode,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

enrol_std <- data.frame(
    enrol_id       = enrol$enrol_id,
    given_name     = enrol$given_name,
    middle_name    = enrol$middle_name,
    surname        = enrol$surname,
    surname_key    = fingerprint(enrol$surname),
    dob            = enrol$dob,
    sex            = sex_code(enrol$sex),
    unit           = enrol$unit,
    street_address = fsquish(paste(enrol$number, enrol$street,
                                    enrol$street_type)),
    suburb         = enrol$suburb,
    postcode       = enrol$postcode,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
str(claims_std, vec.len = 2)
```

## Step 3: block, and know what each pass buys you {#sec-wf-block}

Comparing every enrolment record with every claim is
`r format(50000 * 30000, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)` pairs. Blocking
compares only the records that agree on some key. One key misses every
true match with an error *in that key*, so a linkage runs several passes
with keys that fail in different ways:

| Pass | Key | Survives |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | surname code + exact date of birth | any error in the given name or address |
| 2 | surname code + year of birth | a transposed or shifted date of birth |
| 3 | given-name code + exact date of birth | a changed or misspelled surname |
| 4 | surname code + first initial + postcode | a date of birth that is wholly wrong |

`rLink()` takes those four passes as four `list()`s, and the blocking keys
are written as expressions, so the phonetic code and the date part are
computed inside the call:

```{r}
#| label: blocking
cand <- rLink(
    enrol_std, claims_std,
    block = list(
        surname_dob   = list(soundex(surname), dob),
        surname_year  = list(soundex(surname), format_date(dob, "y")),
        given_dob     = list(soundex(given_name), dob),
        name_postcode = list(soundex(surname), fsubstr(given_name, 1, 1),
                             postcode)
    ),
    # The 1 January placeholder, and the commonest surname codes, would
    # otherwise build blocks that cost more than they can return.
    max_block_size = 2000,
    keep = character()
)
nrow(cand)
table(pass = cand$pass)
```

Because the data carry a truth, each pass can be charged for what it
brought in:

```{r}
#| label: pass-value
truth <- same_person(files, cand$index_1, cand$index_2)
marginal <- t(sapply(sort(unique(cand$pass)), function(p) c(
    candidates = sum(cand$pass == p),
    true_pairs = sum(truth & cand$pass == p),
    yield      = round(mean(truth[cand$pass == p]), 3))))
rownames(marginal) <- paste("pass", sort(unique(cand$pass)))
marginal

c(true_pairs      = true_pair_count(files),
  found           = sum(truth),
  blocking_recall = round(sum(truth) / true_pair_count(files), 4),
  reduction_ratio = round(1 - nrow(cand) /
                          (as.numeric(nrow(enrol_std)) * nrow(claims_std)), 6))
```

Pass 1 does most of the work at a very high yield. Pass 2 is the expensive
one --- it is the only pass that survives a transposed day and month, and
it pays for that with most of the candidates. Passes 3 and 4 add the
records whose surname or date of birth is simply wrong. This table is the
blocking design's justification; a pass that adds no true pairs should be
deleted, and a pass with a very low yield is the one to tighten first.

## Step 4: score each candidate, field by field {#sec-wf-score}

A single similarity over a concatenated name hides which field disagreed.
Score each field separately and keep the columns, so a reviewer can see
*why* a pair scored what it did. `rLink()` puts each score next to the pair
of columns it scores:

A date of birth deserves better than equal-or-not. The errors it actually
carries are a transposed day and month, a year out by one, and the
1 January placeholder --- so grade it, and let the weight apply to the
grade:

```{r}
#| label: dob-agreement
dob_agreement <- function(a, b) {
    da <- fas.Date(a); db <- fas.Date(b)      # comparators are handed text
    pa <- date_parts(da); pb <- date_parts(db)
    ok <- !is.na(da) & !is.na(db)
    gap <- abs(as.numeric(da) - as.numeric(db))
    out <- numeric(length(a))
    # Weakest first; each line overrides the one above it.
    out[which(ok & pa$year == pb$year)]                      <- 0.3
    out[which(ok & pa$year == pb$year & pa$month == pb$month)] <- 0.5
    out[which(ok & gap <= 366)]                              <- 0.7
    out[which(ok & pa$year == pb$year &                      # day/month swap
                   pa$day == pb$month & pa$month == pb$day)]  <- 0.8
    out[which(ok & gap <= 1)]                                <- 0.9
    out[which(ok & da == db)]                                <- 1
    out[!ok] <- 0.5                           # one side missing: no evidence
    out
}
d1 <- c("1985-03-05", "1985-03-14", "1985-03-15", "1985-03-15", "1985-03-15")
d2 <- c("1985-05-03", "1985-03-15", "1986-03-15", "1985-11-02", "1985-03-15")
data.frame(d1, d2, agreement = dob_agreement(d1, d2))
```

```{r}
#| label: scoring
scored <- rLink(
    enrol_std, claims_std,
    block = list(
        list(soundex(surname), dob),
        list(soundex(surname), format_date(dob, "y")),
        list(soundex(given_name), dob),
        list(soundex(surname), fsubstr(given_name, 1, 1), postcode)
    ),
    max_block_size = 2000,
    compare = list(
        surname      = jaro_winkler(surname),
        surname_key  = (function(a, b) as.numeric(a == b))(surname_key),
        given        = jaro_winkler(given_name),
        given_tokens = jaro_winkler_tokens(given_name),
        middle       = (function(a, b)
            ifelse(is.na(a) | is.na(b), 0.5, as.numeric(a == b)))(middle_name),
        dob          = dob_agreement(dob),
        dob_exact    = (function(a, b) as.numeric(a == b))(dob),
        sex          = sex_agree(sex),
        address      = jaro_winkler_tokens(street_address),
        suburb       = jaro_winkler(suburb),
        postcode     = (function(a, b) as.numeric(a == b))(postcode)
    ),
    keep = c("enrol_id", "claim_id", "surname", "given_name", "dob", "sex",
             "street_address", "suburb", "postcode")
)
names(scored)
```

Every carried column takes the suffix of the side it came from, including
the ones only one file has: `enrol_id` is `enrol_id_1` and `claim_id` is
`claim_id_2`. With `score_position = "grouped"` (the default) each score
sits next to the pair of columns it scores, which is what makes a row
readable:

```{r}
#| label: scoring-read
scored[1:3, c("enrol_id_1", "claim_id_2", "surname_1", "surname_2", "surname",
              "given_name_1", "given_name_2", "given", "dob_1", "dob_2",
              "dob", "dob_exact")]
```

Every comparator was probed and oriented so that **1 means an exact
match**, whichever way its own scale runs:

```{r}
#| label: orientation
attr(scored, "compare")
```

That matters as soon as you mix families. Adding an edit *distance* to the
list needs no change to the weights:

```{r}
#| label: orientation-distance
d <- rLink(enrol_std[1:2000, ], claims_std[1:2000, ],
           block = list(list(soundex(surname), dob)),
           compare = list(jw = jaro_winkler(surname),
                          lev = levenshtein(surname),
                          fz = fuzz_token_set_ratio(surname)),
           keep = "surname")
attr(d, "compare")
head(d[, c("surname_1", "surname_2", "jw", "lev", "fz")], 4)
```

`levenshtein()` counts edits (0 is identical) and `fuzz_token_set_ratio()`
runs to 100; both come back on the same 0--1 scale as Jaro-Winkler. Set
`normalise = FALSE` to keep each comparator's own units.

`dob_agreement` is listed as `not detected` in the table above, and that is
the right answer: the probe is a pair of letter strings, which
`fas.Date()` cannot parse, so nothing can be inferred from it and the
scores are passed through untouched. That is harmless here because the
function already returns 0--1 with 1 meaning identical. A comparator of
your own that does *not* already run that way should either be written so
it does or be left to `normalise = FALSE` --- and the `scale` column is
where you check which happened.

### Which fields actually carry information

The weights say how much each field's agreement is worth, and the data can
be asked. For each field, compare its mean score among the pairs that are
the same person with its mean among the pairs that are not --- the
*m*- and *u*-probabilities of the Fellegi-Sunter model, which here can be
computed exactly because the truth is known:

```{r}
#| label: field-information
field_info <- function(column, truth) {
    m <- mean(column[truth]); u <- mean(column[!truth])
    c(agreement_if_match = round(m, 3), agreement_if_not = round(u, 3),
      log_odds = round(log(m / u), 2))
}
truth_c <- same_person(files, scored$index_1, scored$index_2)
t(sapply(list(surname  = pmax(scored$surname, scored$surname_key),
              given    = pmax(scored$given, scored$given_tokens),
              dob      = scored$dob,
              middle   = scored$middle,
              sex      = scored$sex,
              address  = scored$address,
              suburb   = scored$suburb,
              postcode = scored$postcode),
         field_info, truth = truth_c))
```

Two things in that table are worth more than any rule of thumb.

**Surname looks useless, and is not.** Its log-odds is near zero because
*every candidate pair already agrees on the surname code or the given-name
code* --- blocking conditioned on it. A field cannot discriminate among
pairs that were selected for agreeing on it. This is why the naive move of
reading the weights straight off this table misfires, and why a real
project fits the model on the pairs it will actually score, with the
blocking in the model.

**Postcode looks decisive, and is a trap.** Its log-odds is the largest in
the table, because two unrelated people rarely share a postcode. But the
people who *moved* --- one in ten here --- disagree on it while being the
same person. Weighting it by that log-odds buys precision on the easy
pairs and loses exactly the matches that needed help. Address and suburb
carry the same risk for the same reason, and the fix is to weight the
identifiers that do not change (name, date of birth) far above the ones
that do:

```{r}
#| label: weights
w <- c(surname = 3, given = 3, dob = 4, middle = 0.5, sex = 0.5,
       address = 0.75, suburb = 0.25, postcode = 0.5)

scored$score <- with(scored,
    (w["surname"]  * pmax(surname, surname_key) +
     w["given"]    * pmax(given, given_tokens) +
     w["dob"]      * dob +
     w["middle"]   * middle +
     w["sex"]      * sex +
     w["address"]  * address +
     w["suburb"]   * suburb +
     w["postcode"] * postcode) / sum(w))
round(quantile(scored$score, c(0, 0.5, 0.9, 0.99, 1)), 3)
```

`pmax(surname, surname_key)` is the "either kind of agreement will do"
idiom: the Jaro-Winkler score, or 1 if the two fingerprints are identical,
whichever is kinder. The same for the two given-name comparators.

Hand weights are fine for a first pass as long as they are written down
and swept (below). On real data, estimate them: `fastLink` and `reclin2`
fit Fellegi-Sunter weights, including the conditional-independence and
blocking subtleties this section only gestures at.

## Step 5: decide, and admit ambiguity {#sec-wf-decide}

Look at the two score distributions before picking a threshold. If they
overlap, no single cut-off is right and the overlap is the review queue.

```{r}
#| label: distributions
qs <- c(0.001, 0.01, 0.05, 0.25, 0.5)
round(rbind(same_person = quantile(scored$score[truth_c], qs),
            different   = quantile(scored$score[!truth_c], 1 - qs)), 3)
```

Read the second row right to left: the *strongest* non-matches. Where the
weakest true pairs sit above the strongest false ones, a threshold in
between separates them cleanly.

```{r}
#| label: sweep
sweep <- t(sapply(seq(0.70, 0.95, by = 0.025), function(t) {
    keep <- scored$score >= t
    c(threshold = t, links = sum(keep),
      precision = round(mean(truth_c[keep]), 4),
      recall    = round(sum(truth_c & keep) / true_pair_count(files), 4))
}))
sweep
```

A two-threshold rule is more honest than one: accept above the upper,
reject below the lower, and send the band between them to clerical review.
Size that band before promising it to anyone.

```{r}
#| label: review-band
accept <- 0.85
review <- 0.78
band   <- scored$score >= review & scored$score < accept
c(accepted     = sum(scored$score >= accept),
  to_review    = sum(band),
  review_share = round(mean(band), 4),
  review_true  = round(mean(truth_c[band]), 3),
  rejected     = sum(scored$score < review))
```

The band is small --- under 1% of the candidates --- and most of it is
*not* a match. That is the normal shape of a review queue: it holds the
pairs that look like matches on the fields that usually settle it, and a
reviewer's job is mostly to reject them. What the reviewer needs is not
the total but the field that disagreed, which is why the scores were kept
as separate columns rather than summed away:

```{r}
#| label: explain
hard <- scored[band, ][order(-scored$score[band]), ]
fields <- c("surname", "given", "dob", "sex", "address", "suburb", "postcode")
hard[1:4, c("surname_1", "surname_2", "given_name_1", "given_name_2",
            "dob_1", "dob_2", "score")]
round(as.matrix(hard[1:4, ..fields]), 2)
```

And when it is a name that disagrees, `edit_ops()` turns the distance back
into the edits that produced it:

```{r}
#| label: explain-edits
i <- which(hard$given < 1)[1]          # the first pair whose names disagree
hard[i, c("surname_1", "surname_2", "given_name_1", "given_name_2")]
edit_ops(hard$given_name_1[i], hard$given_name_2[i], type = "opcodes")
```

### One-to-one links

If each person should appear once in each file, the pair table needs
resolving: keep each enrolment record's best claim and vice versa.

```{r}
#| label: one-to-one
links <- scored[scored$score >= accept, ]
links <- links[order(-links$score), ]
best  <- links[!duplicated(links$index_1) & !duplicated(links$index_2), ]
c(pairs_above_threshold = nrow(links), one_to_one = nrow(best),
  precision = round(mean(same_person(files, best$index_1, best$index_2)), 4))
```

## Step 6: entity identifiers {#sec-wf-entities}

Downstream work wants one identifier per person, not a list of pairs.
`cluster_pairs()` takes the transitive closure of the accepted pairs;
offset the second file's indices so both files share one numbering:

```{r}
#| label: entities
n1 <- nrow(enrol_std)
entity <- cluster_pairs(best$index_1, best$index_2 + n1,
                        n = n1 + nrow(claims_std))
enrol_std$entity_id  <- entity[seq_len(n1)]
claims_std$entity_id <- entity[n1 + seq_len(nrow(claims_std))]

c(entities = max(entity), records = length(entity))
table(cluster_size = tabulate(entity))
```

Clusters larger than two mean a record was linked to more than one on the
other side, or a chain formed. With a one-to-one resolution they cannot
appear; without one, inspect them before trusting them.

Finally, pseudonymise the identifiers if the linked file is going
anywhere. `fhash()` with a keyed HMAC is stable across runs with the same
key and not reversible without it (@sec-uc-privacy):

```{r}
#| label: pseudonymise
key <- "a-secret-held-by-the-data-custodian"
head(fhash(sprintf("ENT%07d", unique(entity)), algo = "sha256", key = key), 3)
```

## Step 7: what it cost, and what the fast versions bought {#sec-wf-evaluate}

```{r}
#| label: quality
c(enrol = nrow(enrol_std), claims = nrow(claims_std),
  true_pairs = true_pair_count(files),
  pairs_compared = nrow(scored),
  blocking_recall = round(sum(truth_c) / true_pair_count(files), 4),
  precision = round(mean(same_person(files, best$index_1, best$index_2)), 4),
  recall = round(sum(same_person(files, best$index_1, best$index_2)) /
                 true_pair_count(files), 4))
```

`attr(scored, "timings")` says where the time actually went, stage by
stage --- the key stage once per record, the comparators once per pair:

```{r}
#| label: timings
attr(scored, "timings")
```

The standardising in step 2 is a dozen passes over a column each. At
37,500 rows none of them is measurable, so here they are on a million ---
the size at which the choice starts to matter --- against the base R
equivalent:

```{r}
#| label: timing
ms <- function(f, reps = 3) {
    f()                                    # warm up
    start <- Sys.time()
    for (i in seq_len(reps)) f()
    round(1000 * (as.numeric(Sys.time()) - as.numeric(start)) / reps, 1)
}
bench <- function(label, fast, base = NULL) {
    f <- ms(fast)
    b <- if (is.null(base)) NA_real_ else ms(base)
    data.frame(step = label, fast_ms = f, base_ms = b,
               ratio = if (is.na(b)) NA_real_ else round(b / f, 1))
}
big_name <- rep_len(claims$patient_name, 1e6)
big_date <- rep_len(claims$date_of_birth, 1e6)
big_dob  <- rep_len(dob, 1e6)
big_surn <- rep_len(claims_std$surname, 1e6)

do.call(rbind, list(
    bench("upper-case the name",
          function() fupper(big_name), function() toupper(big_name)),
    bench("squish whitespace",
          function() fsquish(big_name),
          function() gsub("[[:space:]]+", " ", trimws(big_name))),
    bench("split on the comma",
          function() fsplit_field(big_name, ",", 1),
          function() vapply(strsplit(big_name, ",", fixed = TRUE), `[`, "", 1L)),
    bench("parse the date of birth",
          function() fas.Date(big_date, format = "dmy"),
          function() as.Date(big_date, format = "%d/%m/%Y")),
    bench("write a Date back as text",
          function() format_date(big_dob),
          function() format(big_dob, "%Y-%m-%d")),
    bench("count vowels per name",
          function() fcount("[AEIOU]", big_name),
          function() lengths(regmatches(big_name,
                                        gregexpr("[AEIOU]", big_name)))),
    bench("Soundex of the surname", function() soundex(big_surn)),
    bench("Jaro-Winkler, a million pairs",
          function() jaro_winkler(big_surn, rev(big_surn)))
))
```

The wins are uneven, and that is the honest picture. The biggest ones are
where base R is doing something structurally expensive: a `strptime()` and
a `strftime()` per element for the dates, a `strsplit()` that allocates a
list of pieces only to take one and throw the rest away, a `gregexpr()`
that allocates a position vector per row only to take its length. Where
base R is already doing one cheap pass in C, the gain is small --- and
@sec-benchmarks lists the cases where base R is the faster choice
outright.

The last two rows have no base R equivalent at all, which is the other
half of the argument: the phonetic key and the similarity score are what
make blocking and scoring possible in the first place, and the pipeline
above is built out of them.
